title: Forces, Acceleration and Motion Equations
description: F=ma, kinematic equations and stopping-distance arithmetic.

method_card.title: Forces, Acceleration and Motion Equations
method_card.content:
Three connected equation families — always identify which one the question is testing before substituting numbers.

Recall equations:

  • \(F = ma\) — force (N) = mass (kg) × acceleration (m/s²)
  • \(a = \Delta v \div \Delta t\) — acceleration = change in velocity ÷ time
  • \(W = mg\) — weight (N) = mass (kg) × gravitational field strength (N/kg)

Given on the equation sheet (Higher Tier only):

  • \(v^2 = u^2 + 2as\) — connects velocity, initial velocity, acceleration and distance
  • (Also on sheet: v = u + at and s = ut + ½at²)

Stopping distance: thinking distance + braking distance. Thinking distance depends on reaction time and speed. Braking distance depends on speed, road conditions and brakes. Examiner reports note students who say crumple zones “absorb force” or “act as a barrier” — the correct explanation is that crumple zones increase the time over which the force acts, reducing peak force on passengers (from F = ma, if time is longer, deceleration is smaller, so force is smaller).

Unit checks: force in N, mass in kg, acceleration in m/s², velocity in m/s, distance in m. Convert km/h to m/s by dividing by 3.6.
steps: Identify the equation: F = ma, a = Δv/Δt, or the kinematic equations (v² = u² + 2as)
List known values with units — check they are in SI units (m, kg, s, N)
Substitute and rearrange algebraically before plugging in numbers
Write the answer with the correct unit
For stopping distance: calculate thinking distance and braking distance separately, then add

exam_context.marks: 2–5 per calculation; crumple zones / safety often 3–6 mark extended response
exam_context.frequency: Very high — forces and motion calculations appear on almost every Physics paper

worked_examples.question: A car of mass 1200 kg accelerates at 3.0 m/s². Calculate the resultant force acting on it.
A cyclist accelerates from 2.0 m/s to 8.0 m/s in 4.0 s. The total mass of cyclist and bike is 80 kg. Calculate the resultant force.
A car travelling at 20 m/s brakes to rest. The braking force is 6000 N and the car has a mass of 1500 kg. Calculate the braking distance. Use v² = u² + 2as.

steps.label: Step 1 — Find deceleration using F = ma
Step 2 — Identify values for v² = u² + 2as
steps.content: v = 0 (comes to rest), u = 20 m/s, a = −4.0 m/s², s = ?

bronze.display: Calculate the force needed to accelerate a 500 kg motorbike at 4.0 m/s².

misconceptions.message: F = ma = 500 × 4.0 = 2000 N. Don't add mass and acceleration.

bronze.display: A 900 kg car has a resultant force of 1800 N acting on it. Calculate its acceleration.

misconceptions.message: a = F ÷ m = 1800 ÷ 900 = 2.0 m/s². Don't divide mass by force.

bronze.display: A resultant force of 4500 N gives a car an acceleration of 3.0 m/s². What is the mass of the car?
A car accelerates from 5 m/s to 25 m/s in 10 s. Calculate its acceleration.

misconceptions.message: Δv = 25 − 5 = 20 m/s. a = 20 ÷ 10 = 2.0 m/s². Don't divide the final velocity by time.

bronze.display: A van of mass 2500 kg has a weight of 24 500 N on Earth. What is the gravitational field strength? Give units.
Which of the following correctly explains why crumple zones reduce injury in a crash?
options: They absorb force like a sponge
They act as a rigid barrier between the car and the engine
They increase the stopping time, reducing the deceleration and the force on passengers

misconceptions.message: Longer stopping time → smaller deceleration (a = Δv/Δt) → smaller force (F = ma). Crumple zones extend the collision time, not block the force.

bronze.display: A truck decelerates from 20 m/s to rest in 8.0 s. Calculate the deceleration.
bronze.equation_hint: \(a = \Delta v \div \Delta t\). The answer will be a deceleration — state it as positive.

misconceptions.message: Δv = 20 − 0 = 20 m/s. a = 20 ÷ 8.0 = 2.5 m/s² deceleration.

bronze.display: A force of 300 N acts on an object that accelerates at 6.0 m/s². Calculate the mass of the object.

silver.display: A 70 kg sprinter accelerates from rest to 9.0 m/s in 3.0 s. Calculate the average resultant force.
silver.equation_hint: First find acceleration using \(a = \Delta v \div t\), then \(F = ma\)

silver.display: A car travelling at 15 m/s applies a braking force of 4500 N. The car has a mass of 1500 kg. Calculate how long it takes to stop.
silver.equation_hint: First find deceleration: \(a = F \div m\), then rearrange \(a = \Delta v \div t\) to find \(t\)

silver.display: A driver takes 0.70 s to react before braking. The car is travelling at 20 m/s. Calculate the thinking distance.
silver.equation_hint: Thinking distance = speed × reaction time. Use \(s = vt\) (no acceleration during thinking phase).

misconceptions.message: During the thinking phase the car travels at constant speed. s = v × t = 20 × 0.70 = 14 m.

silver.display: A car has a thinking distance of 12 m and a braking distance of 36 m at a certain speed. What is its total stopping distance?
silver.equation_hint: Stopping distance = thinking distance + braking distance

misconceptions.message: Stopping distance = 12 + 36 = 48 m.

silver.display: A rocket of mass 20 000 kg produces a thrust of 300 000 N. Its weight is 196 000 N. Calculate the resultant force and the initial acceleration upwards.

misconceptions.message: Resultant force = thrust − weight = 300000 − 196000 = 104000 N. a = F÷m = 104000÷20000 = 5.2 m/s².
Subtract weight from thrust to find net upward force before applying F = ma.

silver.display: A vehicle travelling at 30 m/s decelerates at 5.0 m/s². How far does it travel before stopping? Use v² = u² + 2as.
silver.equation_hint: \(v^2 = u^2 + 2as\). Here v = 0, u = 30, a = −5.0. Rearrange to find s.

misconceptions.message: 0 = 30² + 2×(−5.0)×s → 0 = 900 − 10s → s = 90 m. Deceleration is negative.
Remember to square u: 30² = 900, not 30.

gold.display: A car of mass 1200 kg travelling at 25 m/s stops in 50 m. Calculate the braking force. Use v² = u² + 2as.
A ball is dropped from rest and falls 20 m. Use v² = u² + 2as (g = 9.8 m/s²) to find the speed just before impact. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

misconceptions.message: v² = 0 + 2×9.8×20 = 392. v = √392 = 19.8 m/s (3 s.f.). Don't forget to square-root at the end.
u = 0 (dropped from rest). v² = u² + 2as = 0 + 2×9.8×20 = 392. v = 19.8 m/s.

gold.display: A car is travelling at 72 km/h. Convert this to m/s, then calculate the thinking distance if the reaction time is 0.60 s.

misconceptions.message: 72 km/h ÷ 3.6 = 20 m/s. Thinking distance = 20 × 0.60 = 12 m.
Always convert km/h to m/s (÷ 3.6) before calculating distances in metres.

gold.display: A cyclist and bicycle together have a mass of 75 kg. The cyclist accelerates at 2.0 m/s² against a resistive force of 30 N. What is the driving force from the cyclist's legs?

misconceptions.message: Net force = ma = 75×2.0 = 150 N. Driving force − resistive force = net force → driving = 150 + 30 = 180 N.
F = ma gives the resultant force. Driving force = resultant + resistance = 150 + 30 = 180 N.

gold.display: A car crashes into a wall. Without crumple zones it stops in 0.05 s. With crumple zones it stops in 0.15 s. The car and driver have a combined mass of 1500 kg and are travelling at 15 m/s. Calculate the force with and without crumple zones and find the ratio.

misconceptions.message: Without: a = 15÷0.05 = 300 m/s². F = 1500×300 = 450000 N. With: a = 15÷0.15 = 100 m/s². F = 150000 N. Ratio = 450000÷150000 = 3. Three times greater without crumple zones.
Use a = Δv÷Δt for each scenario, then F = ma. Compare the two forces.

gold.display: A 0.50 kg ball is thrown upward at 14 m/s. Using v² = u² + 2as (g = 9.8 m/s²), calculate the maximum height reached. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

misconceptions.message: At max height, v = 0. 0 = 14² + 2×(−9.8)×s → 0 = 196 − 19.6s → s = 10.0 m (2 s.f.). Acceleration due to gravity is negative (upward throw).
